title: Global urban homogenization and the loss of emotions
research_question: To investigate if homogenized residential peri-urban landscapes trigger different emotional responses when compared to more urban or rural landscapes.

participants.description: 285 participants (41.4% women, 57.2% men, mean age = 46, SD = 17.04, age range = 20-83 years) from Utrecht (Netherlands) and Olten-Aarau (Switzerland). Participants were physically and psychologically healthy, and with normal or corrected-to-normal vision and hearing.
participants.recruitment: Recruited on the street using a mobile virtual reality lab installed in a van. Participants were allowed to participate in a lottery system for a price of 1500 Euros.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Two sets of three 2D 360° Virtual Reality (VR) photos of urban, rural, and peri-urban residential scenes, respectively, for each country (Switzerland and Netherlands). Each scene was combined with ambisonic sound (bird songs, traffic noise) and pre-processed (sharpened, people/cars removed, light corrected).

measures.instrument: Skin conductance responses (ASCL, phasic and tonic signals) measured via electrodes (MTL118F) and Powerlab 8/35 recording device

Questionnaire (gender, age, nationality, income, education, rent, occupation, housing type, ownership, household size, children, length of residence, commuting time, recreation time, working time, neighborhood type)

findings.antecedent: Exposure to peri-urban landscapes (compared to urban and rural landscapes)
findings.mechanism: Homogenized peri-urban landscapes trigger lower emotional responses.
findings.quote: The decay of the phasic signal of the participants that experienced the peri-urban landscapes was lower compared to the other stimuli.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to peri-urban landscapes (compared to urban and rural landscapes)
findings.consequent: Phasic skin conductance signal (area under the curve)
findings.mechanism: Homogenized peri-urban landscapes trigger lower emotional responses.
findings.quote: smaller areas under the curve of the phasic (Friedman test, x²(2) = 16.4, p = 3e-4)

findings.antecedent: Exposure to peri-urban landscapes (compared to urban and rural landscapes)
findings.consequent: Tonic skin conductance signal (area under the curve)
findings.mechanism: Homogenized peri-urban landscapes trigger lower emotional responses.
findings.quote: and the tonic signal (Friedman test, x²(2) = 8.9, p = 1.1e-2) compared to the rural and urban scenes

findings.mechanism: Homogenized peri-urban landscapes are perceived as unpleasant.
findings.quote: SAM valence showed overall negative assessments across the peri-urban scenes

findings.mechanism: Homogenized peri-urban landscapes trigger low arousal.
findings.quote: peri-urban scenes are consistently perceived unpleasant and trigger most of the time a low arousal across the participants and countries.

findings.antecedent: Phasic area (physiological) in rural residential areas
findings.mechanism: Physiological arousal (phasic signal) is linked to place-making in rural contexts.

findings.antecedent: Phasic slope (physiological) in rural residential areas
findings.mechanism: Physiological arousal (phasic signal) is linked to place-making in rural contexts.

findings.antecedent: Social cohesion in rural residential areas
Phasic signal and social cohesion in rural landscapes
findings.quote: In rural landscapes, we observe that place-making is best predicted by the phasic signal and social cohesion (R²-adjusted=0.49, p = 4.3e-4)

findings.antecedent: SAM valence (conscious) in urban residential areas
findings.mechanism: Conscious valence is linked to place-making in urban contexts.

findings.antecedent: Social cohesion in urban residential areas
Place attachment in urban residential areas
Valence, social cohesion, and place attachment in urban landscapes
findings.quote: in urban landscapes, valence comes along with factors related to social cohesion and place attachment (R2-adjusted=0.22, p = 1e-6).

findings.antecedent: Place attachment in peri-urban residential areas
Place attachment (with no influences of physical or stated arousal) in peri-urban landscapes
findings.quote: the peri-urban place-making is only weakly explained by place attachment with no influences of physical or stated arousal (R2-adjusted=0.13, p = 2.7e-4).
we observe no significant differences between place-making across the two case studies conducted in two different countries (Wilcoxon test, W=9190, p=0.55).

findings.mechanism: A 'misfit' between the amount of green and the meanings people ascribe to certain places.
findings.quote: the measured physiological responses are not correlated to the amount of green in the stimuli (Supplementary Table S4), and we even observed lower arousal values despite higher content of greenery

findings.antecedent: Housing situation (rent/ownership), type of housing, working time, and type of neighbourhood lived most of their lives
findings.quote: Only housing situation (rent/ownership), the type of housing, the working time, and the type of neighbourhood where they lived most of their lives had a significant influence on the place-making scores

mechanisms: Homogenized peri-urban landscapes lower people's affective bounds to places and ultimately their intentions to engage with their neighbourhoods.
The dulled emotional responses in peri-urban areas compared to urban and rural areas can be explained by lower social cohesion and place attachment.
Unconscious arousal influences place-making, but social cohesion and place attachment are key factors explaining people's engagement with place.
For individuals to actively engage in place-making, both affective and cognitive processes need to be considered.
moderators: Type of neighbourhood currently living in
Type of neighbourhood grown up in
Type of neighbourhood lived most of life
implementation_implications: Considering emotions is significant in shaping just, equitable, sustainable, and resilient cities.
Reverting urban homogenization processes requires activating people's sense of place, their feeling of caring for their surroundings, and their community engagement.
Planners and policy makers should consider both affective and cognitive processes to foster people's engagement in place-making.
Interventions in the ongoing homogenization process are needed to steer urban transformation towards more liveable environments.

tables.description: Relationships between place-making and emotion-related factors by type of scene (Rural, Urban, Peri-urban) using regression coefficients.

limitations: Temperature and humidity could not be controlled inside the mobile lab.
Scene exposure was limited to two minutes to reduce participant time commitment.
Place-making questions were only asked for the scene most resembling participants' current living place, as pre-tests showed people could only reliably answer if acquainted with the places.
The study is highly context-specific, conducted in two European urban areas.

paper_metadata.title: Global urban homogenization and the loss of emotions
paper_metadata.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Global urban homogenization and the loss of emotions
paper_metadata.crossref_publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractUrban expansion is generating unprecedented homogenization of landscapes across the world. This uniformization of urban forms brings along dramatic environmental, social, and health problems. Reverting such processes requires activating people’s sense of place, their feeling of caring for their surroundings, and their community engagement. While emotions are known to have a modulating effect on behavior, their role in urban transformation is unknown. Drawing on large cognitive-psychological experiments in two countries, we demonstrate for the first time that urban homogenization processes lower people’s affective bounds to places and ultimately their intentions to engage with their neighbourhoods. The dulled emotional responses in peri-urban areas compared to urban and rural areas can be explained by lower social cohesion and place attachment. The findings highlight the significance of considering emotions in shaping just, equitable, sustainable, and resilient cities.
